title: Solo-built a military collection game for the browser (open crates, send expeditions, collect gear up to Mythic) with AI.
author: Professional-Emu4891
selftext:
Hey, I'm the dev of Arsenal Zero, a free military collection game that runs in the browser (crates, expeditions, gear from Common to Mythic). The repo started on Sept 23, real players arrived on Oct 13. Since this sub is about the how, here's the how.

**How AI was used**

* Development: AI-assisted, with Claude Code. Expo / React Native for web, Supabase for the backend.
* Visuals: made with AI. Item and character art with ChatGPT image generation, the short city clips in the tutorial with Runway.
* Translation: the game is in French and English, and the translation is done with AI.
* The video in this post wasn't edited in any video software. It's Remotion, so it's React code (built with Claude Code too), rendering the real in-game items.

**What made the difference: memory, not prompts**

Around week two, the AI kept "forgetting" decisions: a currency in the wrong color, a word I had banned from the UI, a balance rule I'd set two days earlier. What fixed it was a folder of short notes, one decision per file, each with the reason behind it. There are about 130 now: "crystal amounts are always purple", "higher difficulty must always give better loot odds", "never call the player 'recruit'". That's what keeps the game consistent from one session to the next, much more than any clever prompt.

**Server rules in SQL**

Loot rolls, power, rewards: everything runs server-side as Postgres functions, so nobody can edit their save. That's 200+ SQL migrations in a month, written and applied with Claude Code. It bit me once: a migration that worked on dev never made it to production. Now there's a note that says to compare migrations before every deploy.

**Balancing with a simulation**

Before anything touches the economy, a script simulates players over 30 to 60 days (casual, regular, spender) and fails if loot stops getting better with difficulty, or if an event can be cleared in under 7 days. It caught a lot of things I'd never have spotted just by playing.

**Where AI images hurt**

* Style drift. Getting 40+ items to look like they belong to the same game took far more regenerations than I expected.
* One "transparent" PNG came with a fake checkerboard painted into the image. I had to cut it out by hand.
* Some players and communities won't touch AI-made games at all. That's their call, so I only post where it's allowed and say it upfront.

**The part AI made too easy**

When a feature takes one evening, you ship too many. My first real playthrough showed builds, classes, prestige and relics on the very first item you get. Most of my work since launch has been hiding or cutting things, and reading player data: after week one, 224 accounts and 25 people who came back on 3+ different days. The SQL for those analyses is AI-assisted too, which is how I found out that a big chunk of new players were gone within 3 minutes.

**Two questions for you**

* If you use AI art in a live game, how do you keep one style across dozens of assets? Fixed prompts, a reference sheet, img2img from one master image?
* Do you keep your AI's project memory in many small files like this, or in one big rules doc?

**Playable here if you're curious (no download, FR/EN):** [**arsenalzero.com**](https://arsenalzero.com/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=aigamedev)
